plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the cross-ratio, a projective invariant used in single-view 3D scene understanding. It shows sets of collinear points P, Q, and R related by the cross-ratio, projected from a center of projection O. The point R1 lies at infinity because the line connecting the R points is parallel to the line passing through O, P1, and Q1. The figure demonstrates how if two sets of points, related by a projection, have the same ordering, then their cross ratio will be preserved.

interactionPlan.concept: The cross-ratio of four collinear points is invariant under central projection: any line cutting a pencil of four rays through a center O yields the same cross-ratio value, even when one intersection escapes to infinity.
elements: Center of projection O, a large black dot at far left with bold label 'O'
Four black rays emanating from O and extending past the right edge, fanning upward (ray 1 sloping down-right, ray 2 nearly horizontal, ray 3 gently rising, ray 4 steeply rising)
Transversal line 1 (crimson/magenta), a steep near-vertical line on the left crossing all four rays at P1, P2, P3, P4 (bottom to top)
Transversal line 2 (crimson/magenta), a steeply descending line crossing the rays at Q4, Q3, Q2, Q1 (top to bottom)
Transversal line 3 (crimson/magenta), a shallow line descending to the right, crossing rays 4, 3, 2 at R4, R3, R2 and parallel to ray 1 so that R1 never meets it
Black filled dots at every intersection: P1–P4, Q1–Q4, R2–R4
Bold labels P1, P2, P3, P4 placed to the right/below their dots
Bold labels Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 placed to the right of their dots
Bold labels R2, R3, R4 placed above their dots
Annotation at the right end of ray 1: 'R1 → ∞' with an arrow and infinity symbol
Readout panel listing the three cross-ratio values CR(P1,P2;P3,P4), CR(Q1,Q2;Q3,Q4), CR(R1,R2;R3,R4) and the shared invariant value
Optional overlay of signed segment lengths used in the cross-ratio formula
Formula caption: CR = (AC·BD)/(BC·AD)

interactions.teaches: Sliding any transversal (or a single intersection point along its line) changes every individual distance, yet the cross-ratio of each quadruple stays locked to the same number — distances are not invariant, their double ratio is.

Moving the projection center O re-aims the whole pencil and moves all P, Q, R points, yet all three transversals still report one common cross-ratio — the invariance is a property of the projection, not of a special viewpoint.

interactions.label: Orientation of the R transversal (degrees)
interactions.teaches: As the R line rotates toward being parallel to ray 1, R1 slides off to infinity; the cross-ratio does not blow up but smoothly degenerates to a simple ratio of lengths, showing that points at infinity are ordinary members of the projective line.

interactions.label: Show segment lengths and formula terms
interactions.teaches: Seeing the four signed distances that feed (AC·BD)/(BC·AD) makes visible which quantities change wildly and which combination survives.

interactions.label: Highlight quadruple
interactions.teaches: Isolating one transversal at a time shows that each is just a different 'image' of the same four rays, so comparing them is comparing three views of one scene.

demo_steps.title: A pencil of four rays
demo_steps.narration: Four lines radiate from the projection center O. Think of O as a camera pinhole and the rays as sight-lines to four collinear world points.

demo_steps.title: The first cut: P1…P4
demo_steps.narration: A transversal slices the pencil at P1, P2, P3, P4. This quadruple is one 'image' of the scene; its cross-ratio (P1P3·P2P4)/(P2P3·P1P4) is computed and displayed.

demo_steps.title: A second cut gives different distances
demo_steps.narration: The Q transversal cuts the same four rays at very different spacings — every individual length has changed — but the cross-ratio readout is identical.

demo_steps.title: Drag anything you like
demo_steps.narration: Drag the transversals or drag O itself. Lengths, angles and ordering on screen all shift, yet the three cross-ratio numbers stay welded together.

demo_steps.title: Sending R1 to infinity
demo_steps.narration: Rotate the R transversal until it is parallel to ray 1. R1 runs off the page, but the cross-ratio does not break — it simply becomes the ratio R2R3/R2R4 of the remaining points.

demo_steps.title: One invariant, three views
demo_steps.narration: All three quadruples — including the degenerate one containing a point at infinity — share a single number. That number is a measurable property of the 3D scene recoverable from one image.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Central projection destroys lengths, ratios of lengths, and even finiteness — but the double ratio (AC·BD)/(BC·AD) of four collinear points survives every projection, which is why a single photograph can still pin down real metric structure in the world.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape layout. O is a bold black dot at the far left, roughly at mid-height. Four black straight rays fan out from O to the right edge: the lowest slopes gently downward, the next is nearly horizontal, the third rises gently, the fourth rises steeply toward the top-right. Three crimson/magenta transversals cut this pencil: (a) a steep, nearly vertical line in the left third meeting the rays at P1 (bottom) through P4 (top); (b) a steeply falling line in the middle meeting them at Q4 (top) down to Q1 (bottom right of center); (c) a shallow line from upper-left to lower-right that is parallel to the lowest ray, meeting only rays 4, 3, 2 at R4, R3, R2 — with the annotation 'R1 → ∞' plus an arrow and infinity glyph at the right end of the lowest ray. All intersections are large black filled dots with bold serif subscripted labels placed just beside them (P labels to the lower-right, Q labels to the right, R labels above). Add a clean readout panel (neutral gray text, top-right or bottom-left) showing the three cross-ratio values and the formula CR = (AC·BD)/(BC·AD); when values agree, render them in a shared accent color to emphasize equality. Highlighted quadruples should dim the other transversals to light gray. Keep the black/crimson two-color scheme of the original; use white background.
interactionPlan.pedagogicalFraming: Move from 'lengths change' to 'a particular combination of lengths does not', then stress-test that claim by dragging the center and by pushing one point to infinity.

demo_steps.narration: A transversal slices the pencil at P1, P2, P3, P4. This quadruple is one 'image' of the scene; its cross-ratio (P1P3·P2P4)/(P2P3·P1P4) is computed and displayed.

demo_steps.title: A second cut gives different distances
demo_steps.narration: The Q transversal cuts the same four rays at very different spacings — every individual length has changed — but the cross-ratio readout is identical.

demo_steps.title: Drag anything you like
demo_steps.narration: Drag the transversals or drag O itself. Lengths, angles and ordering on screen all shift, yet the three cross-ratio numbers stay welded together.

demo_steps.title: Sending R1 to infinity
demo_steps.narration: Rotate the R transversal until it is parallel to ray 1. R1 runs off the page, but the cross-ratio does not break — it simply becomes the ratio R2R3/R2R4 of the remaining points.

demo_steps.title: One invariant, three views
demo_steps.narration: All three quadruples — including the degenerate one containing a point at infinity — share a single number. That number is a measurable property of the 3D scene recoverable from one image.

plan.keyInsight: Central projection destroys lengths, ratios of lengths, and even finiteness — but the double ratio (AC·BD)/(BC·AD) of four collinear points survives every projection, which is why a single photograph can still pin down real metric structure in the world.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Wide landscape layout. O is a bold black dot at the far left, roughly at mid-height. Four black straight rays fan out from O to the right edge: the lowest slopes gently downward, the next is nearly horizontal, the third rises gently, the fourth rises steeply toward the top-right. Three crimson/magenta transversals cut this pencil: (a) a steep, nearly vertical line in the left third meeting the rays at P1 (bottom) through P4 (top); (b) a steeply falling line in the middle meeting them at Q4 (top) down to Q1 (bottom right of center); (c) a shallow line from upper-left to lower-right that is parallel to the lowest ray, meeting only rays 4, 3, 2 at R4, R3, R2 — with the annotation 'R1 → ∞' plus an arrow and infinity glyph at the right end of the lowest ray. All intersections are large black filled dots with bold serif subscripted labels placed just beside them (P labels to the lower-right, Q labels to the right, R labels above). Add a clean readout panel (neutral gray text, top-right or bottom-left) showing the three cross-ratio values and the formula CR = (AC·BD)/(BC·AD); when values agree, render them in a shared accent color to emphasize equality. Highlighted quadruples should dim the other transversals to light gray. Keep the black/crimson two-color scheme of the original; use white background.
plan.pedagogicalFraming: Move from 'lengths change' to 'a particular combination of lengths does not', then stress-test that claim by dragging the center and by pushing one point to infinity.

discrepancies: The 'R₁ → ∞' annotation sits low along ray 1 in the lower-right of the generated figure, whereas the source places it at the far right edge at roughly R₂'s height with a short arrow; the generated placement puts it close to the Q₁ label and crowds the bottom ray.

Horizontal composition is compressed relative to the source: R₂ lands mid-frame rather than near the right edge, and the P/Q intersection cluster is tighter, so P₄/Q₄/P₃/Q₃/P₂/Q₂ labels sit noticeably closer together than in the original.
Intersection dots are visually smaller and lighter relative to the ray strokes than the source's very heavy black blobs, so the 'four marked points per transversal' reads less emphatically.
Point labels are set at a smaller effective size than the source's large bold serif labels, and the O label hugs the left edge rather than sitting clearly offset from the vertex.

Extra chrome not in the source (cross-ratio readout table, formula header, step narration) occupies the right column; acceptable as UI, but it changes the at-a-glance impression versus the bare geometric figure.
evaluation.notes: A faithful reproduction of the pencil-of-rays / three-transversal cross-ratio figure with correct topology, correct parallel-ray→R₁-at-infinity handling, and a rich, genuinely pedagogical set of interactions (slider, toggles, drag, 6-step demo); main weaknesses are horizontal compression that crowds the P/Q labels, smaller dots/labels than the bold source, and an R₁→∞ annotation placed differently from the original.
action_items: Increase intersection-dot radius and point-label font size (or reduce the viewBox width) so labels and dots read as boldly as the source at inline width.
Move the 'R₁ → ∞' label+arrow toward the right edge near R₂'s vertical level, as in the source, and ensure it never sits within ~40px of the Q₁ label.
Spread the P and Q transversals slightly and push R₂ further right so the P₂/P₃/Q₂/Q₃ label cluster has the same breathing room as the original.
Give the O label a larger offset from the vertex so it does not hug the left frame boundary.
